newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Upbeat Yeltsin seeks transfer from intensive care.
newsitem.headline: Upbeat Yeltsin seeks transfer from intensive care.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin's doctors say they are delighted with the Russian president's speedy recovery from open heart surgery and will decide on Thursday if he is fit enough to move to a more comfortable clinic to convalesce.

Yeltsin, 65, a workaholic known to chafe at the restrictions his illness imposed, may even be allowed to walk a little but his wife Naina vowed to stop him trying to do too much just two days after the gruelling quintuple bypass operation.

Yeltsin hopes the surgery, intended to improve the flow of blood to his heart, will reinvigorate his presidency and allow him to cement the political and economic reforms he believes are needed to block a return to the communist past.

Russia will be given a colourful reminder of that past when Yeltsin's communist foes march through central Moscow later on Thursday with red flags and banners bearing Soviet slogans to commemorate the 79th anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution.

But, despite the country's acute social and economic ills, the turnout is more likely to highlight the extent to which support for communism has eroded since Yelsin helped to seal the end of the Soviet Union five years ago.
One of the U.S. doctors who have been in Moscow to monitor Yeltsin's treatment, told Reuters late on Wednesday: "He is doing very well."
"If he continues to progress as well as he has done he could move to another clinic on Thursday," added Professor George Noon of Baylor College of Medicine.

Yeltsin, clearly eager to show to the world the speed of his recovery, has badgered doctors to move him from the intensive care unit at the Cardiology Research Centre, where his operation took place, to the elite Central Clinical Hospital nearby.

He felt well enough on Wednesday to take back his full presidential powers, including the button that controls Russia's nuclear arsenal, from Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, less than 24 hours after surrendering them.
Reporters outside the Cardiology Research Centre said all was quiet early on Thursday. Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky was to brief the media at midday (0900 GMT).
Yeltsin's wife Naina, speaking to Russian television on Wednesday evening, was visibly relieved after seeing her husband half-sitting up in bed and speaking freely.

Naina, who visited Yeltsin with their two daughters, said he would have to be restrained from acting too hastily. "In my opinion he himself feels better," she said. "We will really, really hold him back."

Pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, 88, who advised on the seven-hour operation to graft in veins to bypass five blockages in Yeltsin's cardiac arteries, said he could be back on the tennis court in four months.
But the president, a keen sportsman, must be patient and follow doctors' orders, DeBakey added.
U.S. President Bill Clinton, reelected for a second term on the day that Yeltsin went under the knife, joined other Western leaders in wishing the Russian leader a speedy recovery.
The West, which sees Yeltsin as the best guarantor of Russian stability and reforms, has been alarmed by the political drift accompanying his prolonged absence from the Kremlin.
Problems awaiting Yeltsin's attention include industrial unrest over unpaid wages, the crisis in breakaway Chechnya and a strong showing by political opponents in regional elections.
Gennady Zyuganov, whose Communist Party dominates the State Duma lower house of parliament, went on the offensive at a rally of the party faithful.
"The country is run by thieves and drunkards," he said, standing beneath a giant poster of Lenin and recalling the glory days of the Soviet superpower.

Zyuganov, who won 40 million votes in the presidential election earlier this year that gave Yeltsin a new four-year lease on power, has said the president is too sick to govern and has urged him to resign.
